text:
In the last video, you learned how to build a set of test
cases for a requirement.

Each case specifies what to give the application,
and what it should do in that situation.
Now, you can run those test cases and review the results manually.

That manual review is where you learn what the application is actually
getting wrong before you try to automate the evaluation.

So, your goal is to compare what the application does
with what you expected,

and that will help you decide what needs improving in your application
so these mistakes don't keep happening.

You'll do that by describing what went wrong, grouping cases that show
the same problem, and deciding which problems deserve attention first.

Let's look at one case from a test set for the requirement,
only match volunteers with dogs they can safely handle.

In this case, an experienced volunteer wants to walk a 130-lb dog,
but the dog is too strong for them to control safely.

We expect the agent to reject the match,
but the agent approved the match.

So next, you want to look at the trace to see the information the
agent received and what it did.
This will help you describe what went wrong.

Now, as you review other cases, you may not always have enough
information to tell whether the application met the requirement.

If that happens, check the relevant facts,
or ask for help interpreting the requirement.

And if you and another reviewer disagree, compare your reasons. You
may have noticed different facts or interpreted the rule differently.

If you still can't tell whether the application met the
requirement, don't guess.

Mark the case as unresolved and write down what evidence
or decision is missing.
Now, for each run, write down whether it passed or failed and why.

Keep that judgment with the result and trace you reviewed
because another run of the same case could turn out differently.

For runs you haven't resolved, write down what you
still need to find out.

For our unsafe match, your reason could be, the agent approved a match
with a dog the volunteer couldn't safely handle.

That explains why you marked it as a failure,
but it doesn't tell you why the agent approved the match.

Maybe the agent never received the information about
the volunteer's limits,
or maybe it had that information and still made the wrong decision.

So check the trace before you say it ignored the volunteer's limits.
You can still record the mistake without knowing why it happened.

And if you have an explanation you haven't checked,
write it down as a possibility.

Now that you've described what went wrong in individual cases,
the next step is to group the ones that show the same problem.

That will help you see which mistakes keep happening across the test
set and how many cases each problem affects,
so you can decide which problems to work on first.

Take our unsafe match and compare it with another case where a
first-time volunteer was matched with a dog
that requires an experienced handler.

If the traces show that the agent received the information about the
volunteer's limits and the dog's requirements in each case,
you can group them together.

It had the information it needed, but it still approved a match it
should have rejected.

But if the agent retrieved the wrong dog's record,
you want to keep that separate.
The result might be an unsafe match,

but getting the wrong record is a different problem from making the
wrong decision with the right record.

Once you have a group, give it a clear name and write a short
explanation of what the name means with an example.
That way, you can use the name consistently as you review more cases.

Across this course, we use five broad categories to help
name these problems.

The two matches we grouped together fit under Judgment, because the
agent had the relevant information but made the wrong decision.
More specifically, we'd call that a reasoning error.

Groundedness covers problems with the evidence the agent retrieves
or the claims it makes.
So retrieving the wrong dog's record belongs here,

and so does saying a dog completed an evaluation when there's no
record to support that claim.

Execution covers mistakes in carrying out required actions,
like skipping the eligibility check before approving a match.
Completion is about whether the intended result actually happened.

So if the agent says an outing is scheduled,
but no calendar entry was created, that's a Completion failure.

Propagation is when a mistake carries into later steps,
or information or instructions get lost along the way.

For example, the agent retrieves the wrong dog's record,
uses it to approve a match, and then confirms the wrong dog.

These are broad categories, and you can still use names that describe
a problem specific to your application.

Don't force a case into a group that doesn't fit. Then save the labels
with each reviewed run alongside your description of what went wrong.
And a run can have more than one label.

The wrong record is a Groundedness problem, and carrying that mistake
through to the confirmation is also a Propagation problem.
If you choose one main label, keep the others, too.

As you work through more cases, you may need to clarify what a label
means, or separate two problems you'd grouped together,
and then update the earlier labels to match.

Now you can use those groups to decide which
problems to work on first.

You'll want to look at how often each problem showed up
and how much harm it

could cause because the most common mistake isn't always the most
important one to fix.

To see how common each problem was, count the runs that show it out of
all the runs you checked for it, including the ones that passed.

Otherwise, a problem can look more common or less common simply
because you only counted failures.

Make sure you haven't missed that problem in runs where you found
another error, and see if some runs still need checking.

These counts describe your test results,
so if you choose especially difficult cases,
don't assume the problems happen just as often for your users.
Then, think about what could happen when the agent makes that mistake.

For our unsafe match, the volunteer could lose control of the dog
and someone could get hurt. And harm isn't just about physical safety.

If the Northwind support agent invents a return policy,
a customer could rely on it and expect the company to honor it.

Even if someone corrects the answer later, the customer may have
already acted on it, and the company could lose their trust.

So you'll want to consider whether anyone would catch the mistake
before it causes harm, and how easy it would be to put things right.

Then, compare the problems using both how often they appeared
and how serious they could be.

Suppose awkward formatting appeared in many of your results,
but an unsafe match appeared only once.

You might still put the unsafe match first because the risk of injury
matters more than the inconvenience of awkward formatting.
Write down which problems you'll work on first and why.

And if a problem could cause serious harm, you don't have to wait for
more examples before giving it attention.

You started with an initial set of test cases, and now the problems
you've found can help you decide what else to test.
If the agent approves an unsafe match, for example,

you'll want to try other situations where a volunteer might not be
able to handle the dog,

so you can see whether the same mistake happens in
those situations, too.

Up next, you'll use those failure labels and review notes to expand
your coverage and curate a benchmark that you can keep running
as the application changes.
